explain: Delay lines up the arrivals behind the array, and the polarity flip makes them cancel there.

q: Why do gradient cardioid sub arrays usually need EQ on the front response?
options: Because the rear sub adds +6 dB at every frequency
Because the front sum falls away at low frequencies where the spacing is a small fraction of a wavelength
explain: At low frequencies the inverted rear sub arrives almost in time with the front sub, so they partly cancel in front too. The front sum peaks near d = λ/4.

q: In an end-fire sub array, which way do the subwoofers face?
explain: All end-fire elements face forward with the same polarity. Only spacing and delay create the directivity.

q: Roughly how far does sound travel in air in 2.9 ms?
explain: At about 343 m/s, sound covers about 0.343 m per millisecond, so 2.9 ms ≈ 1 m.

q: Two radio mics transmit on 550.000 MHz and 550.400 MHz. Where are their third-order intermodulation products?
explain: 2 × 550.000 − 550.400 = 549.600 and 2 × 550.400 − 550.000 = 550.800 MHz. Sums and differences like 1100.4 and 0.4 MHz are second-order and far outside the band.

q: Three transmitters are set to 600.0, 600.5 and 601.0 MHz. Which third-order product lands exactly on one of the carriers?
explain: With equal spacing, 2f2 − f1 = f3, so 601.0 MHz is hit. 599.5 and 602.0 MHz are real products but fall outside the plan; equal spacing is what makes 601.0 MHz clash.

q: In the ideal model, both carriers feeding a non-linear stage rise by 2 dB. Roughly how much do the third-order products rise?
explain: Third-order products rise about 3 dB per 1 dB of input, so 2 dB more input gives about 6 dB more product. They grow faster than the wanted signals.

q: How many two-transmitter third-order products (of the 2f1 − f2 type) do 4 transmitters produce?
explain: Each ordered pair gives one product: N(N − 1) = 4 × 3 = 12. The trap is counting unordered pairs (6), but each pair makes two products.

q: Why are in-ear monitor transmitters a common source of intermodulation problems?
options: They transmit only in short bursts
They use a different modulation that cannot mix
They run continuously at relatively high power and are often installed close together
explain: Continuous, stronger carriers close together produce strong IMD. Use a combiner and keep transmit antennas apart from receive antennas.

q: After the 700 MHz band was reassigned to mobile services in the EU, where does the UHF TV band used by many radio mics end?
explain: The EU TV band now runs from 470 to 694 MHz. Exact use for wireless mics depends on national rules.

q: What is intermodulation in a wireless system?
options: Audio feedback between a mic and a wedge
New frequencies created when two or more signals mix in a non-linear stage
Loss of signal caused by a body blocking the antenna
explain: Non-linear circuits mix carriers and produce sums and differences of their multiples, which can land on channels in use.

q: A porous panel plus its air gap reaches 0.20 m from a rigid wall (c = 343 m/s). Using the quarter-wavelength rule, down to roughly what frequency does it work well?
explain: λ/4 = 0.20 m means λ = 0.80 m, so f = 343 / 0.80 ≈ 429 Hz. Below that, absorption falls off gradually.

q: A quadratic residue diffuser uses N = 7. What is its well-depth sequence (s = n² mod 7, n = 0 to 6)?
explain: Squares 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36 taken mod 7 give 0, 1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 1. The sequence is symmetric, which is a property of quadratic residues.

q: You place a 5 cm porous panel directly on a rigid wall to tame a 100 Hz mode. Why does it do almost nothing?
options: Porous material only absorbs above 10 kHz
At the wall particle velocity is near zero, and λ/4 at 100 Hz is about 0.86 m away
The panel reflects 100 Hz back with more energy
Porous absorbers need to be in the centre of the room to work
explain: Porous absorbers need moving air. At 100 Hz the velocity maximum is about 0.86 m from the wall, far beyond a 5 cm panel.

q: Where does a membrane (pressure-based) bass trap work best?
options: In the middle of the room
Hanging from the ceiling at the listening position
At boundaries and corners, where pressure is high
A quarter wavelength from the wall
explain: Membrane traps respond to pressure, which is highest at boundaries and especially in corners, where every room mode has a pressure maximum.

q: What is the main difference between a diffuser and an absorber?
options: A diffuser removes energy; an absorber spreads it
A diffuser scatters reflections in many directions; an absorber turns energy into heat
They are the same thing with different names
explain: Diffusers keep the energy in the room but break up strong reflections. Absorbers reduce the reflected energy.

q: What does an absorption coefficient of 1.0 mean at a given frequency?
options: All the sound energy hitting the surface is reflected
Half the sound energy is absorbed
The surface diffuses all the sound
All the sound energy hitting the surface is absorbed
explain: α ranges from 0 (all reflected) to 1 (all absorbed) and changes with frequency.

q: Why are thin foam tiles not enough to control bass in a small studio?
options: They are too thin to reach the high-velocity region of low-frequency waves
Foam only absorbs at exactly 1 kHz
Foam reflects bass louder than bare walls
Bass is controlled only by EQ
explain: Low frequencies have long wavelengths, so porous material needs much more depth from the wall to absorb them.

q: An FM patch has a 200 Hz modulator and a peak deviation of 600 Hz. Using Carson's rule, what is the approximate bandwidth?
explain: Carson's rule: 2(Δf + fm) = 2(600 + 200) = 1600 Hz. The index here is 600 / 200 = 3.

q: In simple FM with a sine carrier and sine modulator, the carrier component disappears at a modulation index of about 2.4. Why?
options: The modulator becomes louder than the carrier
The carrier's amplitude follows the Bessel function J0, which crosses zero near 2.405
The sidebands fold back and cancel the carrier at any index above 2
The synth's filter removes the fundamental
explain: Each component's amplitude follows a Bessel function of the index. J0 governs the carrier and is zero at about 2.405.

q: A granular instrument plays 50 ms grains at a density of 40 grains per second. On average, how many grains overlap at any moment?
explain: Overlap = size × density = 0.05 s × 40 /s = 2. A new grain starts every 25 ms while each lasts 50 ms.

q: Which carrier-to-modulator ratio gives an inharmonic, bell-like FM spectrum?
explain: Non-integer ratios put sidebands at frequencies that are not multiples of a common fundamental. Integer ratios give harmonic spectra.

q: How does a granular instrument stretch a sound to twice its length without changing pitch?
options: It plays the whole sample at half speed
It moves the read position through the source at half speed while each grain plays at its original pitch
It lowers the grain size to 1 ms
It adds reverb to fill the gaps
explain: Read position and grain playback rate are independent, so time and pitch can be controlled separately. Half-speed playback would drop the pitch by an octave.

q: In FM synthesis, which control most directly makes the sound brighter?
explain: Raising the index pushes energy into more sidebands, which brightens the tone.

q: What is a typical grain length in granular synthesis?
options: Exactly one cycle of the source
explain: Grains are short, usually from about 1 to 100 ms, and each is shaped by a smooth window.

q: Your session is on a two-disk RAID 1 in the studio, and a second copy is on a USB drive on the same desk. Does this meet the 3-2-1 rule?
options: Yes, because RAID 1 already counts as two copies
Yes, because there are three physical disks
No, because USB drives cannot be used for backup
No: the RAID mirror is effectively one copy, and nothing is off site
explain: A mirror reflects deletions and corruption instantly, so it counts as one copy. A fire or theft in the room would also take both remaining copies.

q: You accidentally delete a project folder from a folder that syncs to a cloud service with no version history. What is the most likely result?
options: The deletion syncs and the cloud copy is removed too
The cloud keeps the folder because sync only uploads
The deleted folder is restored automatically at the next sync
explain: Sync mirrors changes, including deletions. That is why sync without versioning is not a backup.

q: After copying a day's recordings to two drives, which check best confirms that each copy is identical to the card?
options: Comparing checksums (e.g. MD5 or xxHash) of source and copies
Checking that the file count matches
Opening one file and listening to the start
explain: Only a hash comparison shows every bit is the same. Size and file count can match while data inside is corrupted.

q: Which file name sorts correctly by date in any file browser?
explain: YYYY-MM-DD (ISO 8601) puts the largest unit first, so alphabetical order is also chronological.

q: Why should you print or commit plugin-processed tracks before handing over a session?
options: It makes the session open faster on the same machine
The recipient may not have the same plugins or versions, so the sound could change
Plugins are not allowed in delivered sessions
Printing tracks improves their sample rate
explain: Missing or different plugin versions change or bypass the processing. A printed track keeps the sound you approved.

q: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule ask for?
options: Three drives, two computers and one cloud account
Backups every 3 days, kept 2 weeks, 1 restore test a year
Three copies, on two different types of storage, with one off site
Three versions of each mix, two stems and one master
explain: Three copies, two media types, one off site: so no single failure or disaster can destroy all your work.

q: Which item belongs in a session handover note?
options: A list of unused takes deleted from the session
Sample rate, frame rate and start timecode
explain: The recipient needs the technical settings to open, sync and continue the session correctly.
